evidence.quote: A 58-year-old male was admitted to the Emergency Department of the Civico Hospital of Partinico (Italy) in February 2025 with acute severe respiratory distress. His medical history included morbid obesity (BMI > 45), chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), bronchiectasis, chronic respiratory failure on home non-invasive ventilation and nocturnal oxygen therapy, ischemic heart disease secondary to long-standing hypertension, type 2 diabetes mellitus, and chronic venous insufficiency. His home medications comprised a sodium–glucose cotransporter-2 inhibitor, a GLP-1 receptor agonist, low-dose aspirin, a statin, omega-3 fatty acids, a proton-pump inhibitor, an ACE inhibitor, a venotonic agent, long-acting insulin, and an antihyperuricemic drug. He was regularly vaccinated against Streptococcus pneumoniae, SARS-CoV-2 (four doses), and seasonal influenza.

Arterial blood gas analysis showed severe respiratory acidosis with marked hypercapnia. Laboratory tests revealed leukocytosis, elevated C-reactive protein, and normal procalcitonin levels. Because of worsening dyspnea and declining mental status, the patient was sedated, intubated, and mechanically ventilated. Lung-protective ventilation was instituted according to ARDSNet recommendations (), but gas exchange remained severely impaired, consistent with refractory hypoxemic and hypercapnic respiratory failure. The patient was therefore admitted to the intensive care unit (ICU) for ongoing management.

Antimicrobial therapy was maintained according to susceptibility results until full recovery. The patient’s clinical condition continued to improve over the following days, allowing discontinuation of renal replacement therapy and, on day 9, successful extubation after a spontaneous breathing trial (Figure 2). He was transferred to a medical ward and later discharged home in stable condition after full respiratory recovery. A summary of the patient’s clinical course, major interventions, and outcomes is presented in Table 1.

items.subject: index_patient

evidence.quote: findings compatible with bilateral viral pneumonia

A few hours after ICU admission, results from the syndromic multiplex PCR assay (BioFire® FilmArray®) performed on the BAL became available, revealing exclusive positivity for human metapneumovirus type 1. Over the following 48 h, the patient’s condition deteriorated further. He developed viral septic shock with profound hemodynamic instability requiring continuous vasopressor support. Persistent anuria and rising azotemia prompted the initiation of continuous renal replacement therapy.

Approximately 72 h after admission, the patient’s respiratory and hemodynamic parameters began to improve. BAL cultures subsequently grew Streptococcus pneumoniae, not detected by the initial multiplex PCR, confirming bacterial superinfection. Serologic pneumococcal vaccine seroconversion and pneumococcal strain typing were not performed, as these analyses are not routinely available in our institution. The multiplex respiratory PCR panel was negative for all other viruses and atypical bacteria, and blood cultures remained negative, supporting hMPV-1 infection as the primary cause of respiratory failure.

claims.text: A 58-year-old man with morbid obesity (BMI >45), COPD, bronchiectasis and chronic respiratory failure on home NIV/nocturnal oxygen, plus ischemic heart disease, hypertension, diabetes and venous insufficiency, presented in February 2025 with severe respiratory distress, GCS 9, cyanosis, paradoxical breathing, anuria and wheezing. Baseline pH was 7.0, PaCO2 124 mmHg, P/F approximately 124, WBC 12,900/mm³, CRP 11 mg/dL and normal procalcitonin. Sedation, intubation and ARDSNet ventilation did not initially correct refractory hypoxemic/hypercapnic failure. CT showed right consolidation/air bronchograms and left-upper-lobe ground-glass/tree-in-bud changes. BAL multiplex PCR was initially exclusively positive for hMPV-1; other panel viruses/atypical bacteria and blood cultures were negative. Empiric piperacillin–tazobactam/vancomycin were started. Over 48 hours he developed viral septic shock with MAP approximately 35 mmHg, norepinephrine increased to 1 μg/kg/min, creatinine rising from 1.4 to 2.9 mg/dL and hyperkalemia. CRRT and prednisone 25 mg/day began on day 2, when vancomycin was stopped for suspected nephrotoxicity. Empiric coverage was adjusted to imipenem/cilastatin, whose exact switch day is unstated. Fluconazole was preferred during CRRT, without a documented regimen. Respiratory/hemodynamic parameters improved around 72 hours; subsequent BAL culture confirmed pneumococcal superinfection despite initial PCR non-detection and prior vaccination. Serotyping and vaccine seroconversion testing were not performed; viral-load quantification was not reported. CRRT stopped on day 5 while anuria persisted. Successful SBT/extubation occurred on day 9, followed by ward transfer and stable home discharge/full respiratory recovery on day 14. Follow-up CT improved and the patient reported no long-term complications; precise imaging/patient-perspective dates and renal recovery course are unreported.

His medical history included morbid obesity (BMI > 45), chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), bronchiectasis, chronic respiratory failure on home non-invasive ventilation and nocturnal oxygen therapy, ischemic heart disease secondary to long-standing hypertension, type 2 diabetes mellitus, and chronic venous insufficiency. His home medications comprised a sodium–glucose cotransporter-2 inhibitor, a GLP-1 receptor agonist, low-dose aspirin, a statin, omega-3 fatty acids, a proton-pump inhibitor, an ACE inhibitor, a venotonic agent, long-acting insulin, and an antihyperuricemic drug. He was regularly vaccinated against Streptococcus pneumoniae, SARS-CoV-2 (four doses), and seasonal influenza.

Because of worsening dyspnea and declining mental status, the patient was sedated, intubated, and mechanically ventilated. Lung-protective ventilation was instituted according to ARDSNet recommendations (), but gas exchange remained severely impaired, consistent with refractory hypoxemic and hypercapnic respiratory failure. The patient was therefore admitted to the intensive care unit (ICU) for ongoing management.

A few hours after ICU admission, results from the syndromic multiplex PCR assay (BioFire® FilmArray®) performed on the BAL became available, revealing exclusive positivity for human metapneumovirus type 1. Over the following 48 h, the patient’s condition deteriorated further. He developed viral septic shock with profound hemodynamic instability requiring continuous vasopressor support. Persistent anuria and rising azotemia prompted the initiation of continuous renal replacement therapy.

Approximately 72 h after admission, the patient’s respiratory and hemodynamic parameters began to improve. BAL cultures subsequently grew Streptococcus pneumoniae, not detected by the initial multiplex PCR, confirming bacterial superinfection. Serologic pneumococcal vaccine seroconversion and pneumococcal strain typing were not performed, as these analyses are not routinely available in our institution. The multiplex respiratory PCR panel was negative for all other viruses and atypical bacteria, and blood cultures remained negative, supporting hMPV-1 infection as the primary cause of respiratory failure.

evidence.quote: A 58-year-old male was admitted to the Emergency Department of the Civico Hospital of Partinico (Italy) in February 2025 with acute severe respiratory distress. His medical history included morbid obesity (BMI > 45), chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), bronchiectasis, chronic respiratory failure on home non-invasive ventilation and nocturnal oxygen therapy, ischemic heart disease secondary to long-standing hypertension, type 2 diabetes mellitus, and chronic venous insufficiency. His home medications comprised a sodium–glucose cotransporter-2 inhibitor, a GLP-1 receptor agonist, low-dose aspirin, a statin, omega-3 fatty acids, a proton-pump inhibitor, an ACE inhibitor, a venotonic agent, long-acting insulin, and an antihyperuricemic drug. He was regularly vaccinated against Streptococcus pneumoniae, SARS-CoV-2 (four doses), and seasonal influenza.

Arterial blood gas analysis showed severe respiratory acidosis with marked hypercapnia. Laboratory tests revealed leukocytosis, elevated C-reactive protein, and normal procalcitonin levels. Because of worsening dyspnea and declining mental status, the patient was sedated, intubated, and mechanically ventilated. Lung-protective ventilation was instituted according to ARDSNet recommendations (), but gas exchange remained severely impaired, consistent with refractory hypoxemic and hypercapnic respiratory failure. The patient was therefore admitted to the intensive care unit (ICU) for ongoing management.

Antimicrobial therapy was maintained according to susceptibility results until full recovery. The patient’s clinical condition continued to improve over the following days, allowing discontinuation of renal replacement therapy and, on day 9, successful extubation after a spontaneous breathing trial (Figure 2). He was transferred to a medical ward and later discharged home in stable condition after full respiratory recovery. A summary of the patient’s clinical course, major interventions, and outcomes is presented in Table 1.
